name: Bilal Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, which has no ties to insurers, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a usual day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the policy renewal desk at an insurer, with a bachelor's degree and seven years of practice behind me. I assign files, check exclusions against old policies, and call the branch when a form makes no sense. The work is orderly until one missing date makes a customer's cover uncertain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you take pride in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a plain checklist and the newer staff know they can bring me a confusing form. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer to understand the rule myself. My pay is high for this desk, and I have more than a year of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the existing renewal checks and use any saved minutes to clear the backlog. A shortcut that misses an exclusion costs more than it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job and salary look secure for the next few years. The insurer needs someone to answer for mistakes, and I have savings plus several other insurers nearby, although a junior vacancy might go unfilled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep my written checklist and count the corrections that come back each month. In the first year of this mild change I'd stay in my paid lead role and show the manager where the backlog still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I do not see a reason to change a system that is working, though I notice how quickly an empty chair becomes normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The branch manager called twice last week about dates entered wrong. I would use those examples if someone says the clerk can simply disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fund a new tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not spend my savings on a new tool for the company. A reserve is for my own rent and a possible gap in wages, not the insurer's equipment.

say: I'd keep **renewal checks** and clear the backlog with saved time.
I'd show the manager **correction records** before posts are removed.
think: My **lead pay** looks secure over the next few years.
I worry a **junior vacancy** may stay empty, even in mild change.
do: Count **returned corrections** against the written checklist each month.
Keep my **paid lead role** in the first year of mild change.
feel: **Calm** about his own pay, alert to empty desks.
S0.quote: A reserve is for my own rent and a possible gap in wages, not the insurer's equipment.
fieldNote: His **written checklist** reflects skill and caution, not inability to use technology.
His **year-plus cushion** and many local insurers make current income feel secure.
He notices the **junior vacancy** without assuming his own post is next.

steps.text: Count returned policy corrections against his checklist each month
Continue paid lead renewal work during the first year of mild change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that automatic letters still need a person to stand behind them. If software writes, checks and answers the policy questions, it reaches the heart of our desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could fall if headquarters joins two renewal teams. I earn enough to save and have more than a year put away, yet I would hate seeing my skill priced as a few minutes of software review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take a month of correction records to our manager and ask for the new staffing numbers. In the first year after the change, if my paid hours fall, I'd contact two nearby insurers about advertised lead clerk openings before leaving this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, not destitute. I know I have a cushion, but I would rather use it to choose than to pay rent while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try an approved tool if my employer required it and showed me how errors are checked. I would not start using a public AI site on customer files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for another insurer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other insurers in town, but an advert is not an offer. I would check the pay and hours on paper before giving notice here.

say: I'd say automatic **policy letters** still need a named reviewer.
I'd ask management for **staffing numbers** before accepting claims of efficiency.
think: My **paid hours** could fall if teams merge.
My **savings cushion** helps me choose, but cannot replace wages forever.
do: Bring **one month of corrections** to the manager now.
Contact **two nearby insurers** if paid hours fall, checking written pay and hours before notice.
Try an **approved AI tool** only if required at work and its errors are explained.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, despite a strong reserve.
S1.quote: There are other insurers in town, but an advert is not an offer.
fieldNote: He would learn a **required approved tool** once errors and customer privacy are explained.
His **hours risk** comes from consolidation, not immediate certainty of dismissal.
He checks **written pay and hours** before moving employers.

steps.text: Bring one month of policy correction records to management
Contact two nearby insurers if hours fall; verify written pay and hours before notice
Try employer-required AI tool at work after learning its error checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could do the reasoning on policy forms, and our office would feel it then. Robots that arrive around 2031 do not delay a desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my post if the insurer decides AGI can handle renewals without a lead clerk. I do not know their decision yet; my year of savings and the other insurers nearby let me consider a search without pretending a new wage is assured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a written account of staffing plans and set aside the next bonus if it is actually paid. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply to advertised paid policy review jobs, check their pay and eligibility rules, and claim public support only if I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The work could leave quickly, but I have time and money for a careful search rather than a rushed gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a quick qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not spend my savings on a course that promises a new career in two years. I would first ask what qualification a posted job requires and whether it pays enough for my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner cover the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner the savings are mine to bridge a gap, not a reason to sign a more expensive lease. My partner earns now, but I do not know what that income would be after 2028.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches policy reasoning before robots.
I'd request a **written staffing plan** before the insurer changes posts.
think: I **could lose my post**, though management has not decided yet.
My year of savings helps, but **another wage** is not assured.
do: Request a **written staffing plan** while still paid.
Save the next **actual bonus** if it is paid.
Apply for **paid review jobs** meeting qualifications and rent, then claim eligible support if displaced after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about possible job loss, with a workable cushion.
S2.quote: I could lose my post if the insurer decides AGI can handle renewals without a lead clerk.
fieldNote: He treats dismissal as a **possibility**, not a settled outcome.
He will save a **bonus only if paid** and seek support only if eligible.
He does not assume **partner income** will cover a future gap.

steps.text: Save his next bonus only if it is paid
Apply for advertised paid review jobs meeting qualifications and rent after job loss
Claim eligible public support during any job search after dismissal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us time to count what policy work remains worth paying for. Robots around 2034 have almost nothing to do with this office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The insurer could reduce the desk before 2031, but I am still drawing my high lead pay now. I have several local employers to ask, though none owes me a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the coming year I'd keep a record of exclusions corrected by a person and check posted lead clerk jobs twice a year. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if this role loses paid hours, I'd apply to a posted insurer job only after confirming the salary and qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I may lose paid hours before 2031, though savings give me time to search without losing next month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an approved new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager which cases still need a human signature, and I would listen to the answer. If a new system becomes required, I will learn it at work, but I need to see its checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a compliance course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A compliance course might be useful if a real advert demands it. I would check the course cost and entry rules before paying, not enrol just to feel busy.

say: I'd show **corrected exclusions** before letting people call the desk redundant.
I'd say **2034 robots** do not protect office paperwork.
think: My **lead pay** continues now, though hours may later shrink.
I can ask several nearby employers about **real openings**, but none owes me a paid vacancy.
do: Record **human-corrected exclusions** during the coming year.
Apply to **posted paid insurer jobs** after 2031 only if hours fall and salary and qualifications fit.
Learn a **required approved AI tool** at work only after its checks are shown.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hours loss before 2031, with a savings cushion.
S3.quote: I have several local employers to ask, though none owes me a vacancy.
fieldNote: He uses **correction records** to make human work visible.
He would learn a **required tool** at work after seeing its checks.
Course fees require **real job criteria** before he commits money.

steps.text: Record policy exclusions corrected by clerks during coming year
Apply to posted paid insurer jobs meeting salary and qualifications if hours fall
Learn required employer AI tool at work after seeing its checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 is a long enough warning to review our staffing each year. The robots around 2039 are still not what changes our policy forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My salary and lead role look secure in the next few years. I cannot know the office in 2036, but at 37 I could still have decades of paid work ahead, so I will not pretend retirement is the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep leading renewals and review my savings against twelve months of expenses every quarter. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my paid role still exists, I'd continue it; if it closes, I'd search advertised paid insurer posts before spending on any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. A decade gives me time to watch actual staffing decisions and make a sensible move if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family or a business be your backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask my family to cover my living costs or buy a business to escape a date on a card. I earn well now and can keep a reserve for a real job gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach new clerks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep teaching new clerks how to read an exclusion in the original policy. If new clerks only copy a summary, nobody can tell a customer why the cover changed.

say: I'd ask management for **annual staffing reviews** so clerks hear specific dates and numbers as 2036 approaches.
I'd keep teaching **original-policy checks** to new clerks.
think: My **near-term lead role** and salary look secure.
I cannot treat a distant **retirement** as my plan at 37.
do: Review **twelve-month savings** against expenses each quarter.
Keep **paid renewal work** after 2036 if the role exists.
Search **advertised paid insurer posts** if the role closes.
feel: **Calm** about his near-term work and money.
S4.quote: If new clerks only copy a summary, nobody can tell a customer why the cover changed.
fieldNote: He has **year-plus savings** and a secure near-term lead salary.
He rejects assumed **family support** and premature retirement.
He keeps teaching **original-policy reading** while work exists.

steps.text: Review his savings against twelve months of expenses quarterly
Continue paid policy renewal work if role exists after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my skill could be priced out before I know which desk still needs it. Written staffing plans, real paid openings with clear pay and temporary support I qualify for would help if I am cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tells a customer why a renewal changed. Someone must read the original policy and answer in plain words. A fast letter is no service if nobody can explain the exclusion.

headlineQuote: A fast letter is no service if nobody can explain the exclusion.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old policy lead** with a bachelor's degree and seven years of renewal practice.
He earns **higher pay**, has more than a year of expenses saved and several nearby insurers to consider.
He has **never used AI**, trusting a written checklist and direct answers to customers.
The plateau feels **calm**; possible cuts to his own paid hours make faster worlds anxious or uneasy.
He checks **advertised pay and qualifications** before any move and never assumes partner or family income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could price out his policy skill before he finds another paid desk.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan** and advertised openings with clear wages would help.
Temporary **support he qualifies for** could bridge a real job gap.
